claims.claim: Any user upload that a browser can render as HTML or SVG runs script in the origin that serves it.
claims.evidence_quote: serving user-controlled content on a GitHub.com domain would increase the chances of script execution on that domain

claims.claim: If that origin is your app, the uploader has stored XSS.
claims.evidence_quote: Client-side active content (XSS, CSRF, etc.) that could endanger other users if the files are publicly retrievable

claims.claim: Serve uploads from `example-usercontent.com` (a different eTLD+1), not `files.example.com`.
claims.evidence_quote: we serve all responses to raw requests on their own domain

claims.claim: Subdomains share cookies scoped to `.example.com` and count as same-site (SameSite cookies and CSRF defences treat them as trusted).
Per-user/tenant subdomains (`alice.example-pages.com`) need the domain on the **Public Suffix List** so each subdomain is its own site.
Examples: GitHub (`githubusercontent.com`), Google (`googleusercontent.com`).
Content-Type: <type detected server-side, never the client's>
claims.evidence_quote: The Content-Type for uploaded files is provided by the user, and as such cannot be trusted, as it is trivial to spoof

claims.claim:
Content-Type: <type detected server-side, never the client's>
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
claims.evidence_quote: We also mitigate this by using the X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff header, but CSP provides extremely strong assurances, even if there were a bug that let an attacker control content-type

claims.claim: Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="..."          (inline only for allowlisted image/video types)
Content-Security-Policy: sandbox; default-src 'none'; img-src 'self'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'
Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: cross-origin               (or same-site if only your app embeds them)
`CSP: sandbox` gives the document an opaque origin with scripts disabled even if it is rendered.
SVG can contain `<script>`, event handlers and `<foreignObject>`.
rasterise to PNG on upload (safest)
claims.evidence_quote: decode and re-encode to an allowed image format, explicitly removing unnecessary metadata

claims.claim: sanitise with DOMPurify's SVG profile
scripts do not run in ``-loaded SVG, but direct navigation does
HTML uploads: never inline on any domain you care about; attachment only or render in a sandboxed iframe from the sandbox domain
Private files via short-lived signed URLs (S3/GCS presigned GET, CloudFront signed URLs) tied to the requesting user
never long-lived public object URLs for private data
Uploading `<svg onload=alert(document.domain)>` and opening its URL directly shows the sandbox domain (or no execution), never your app's domain.
App cookies are absent from requests to the content domain.

coverage: I extracted every concrete claim in the skill in file order - the HTML/SVG script-execution and stored-XSS statements, the separate-domain recommendation with its cookie/same-site and Public Suffix List rationale and the GitHub/Google domain examples, all five response-header lines plus the CSP sandbox opaque-origin behaviour, the SVG script/foreignObject/DOMPurify/rasterise/img-navigation behaviours, the HTML-upload sandboxed-iframe rule, the signed-URL access-control rules and both Verify checks - and checked each against the three listed sources, all of which I fetched and read.
suggested_edits: Nothing is contradicted, but many material claims have no coverage in the listed sources: add sources for CSP sandbox opaque-origin semantics, Content-Disposition, Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy, cookie domain scope and same-site semantics, the effect of Public Suffix List listing on per-user subdomains (publicsuffix.org only defines public suffixes and mentions supercookies), SVG script/foreignObject content and img-loaded SVG behaviour, DOMPurify's SVG profile, and S3/GCS/CloudFront presigned or signed URLs. The Google googleusercontent.com example appears in no listed source (GitHub's githubusercontent.com is evidenced by the raw.githubusercontent.com redirect in the github.blog post), so cite a source for it or drop it. The listed sources do confirm the core separation, content-type, nosniff and image re-encoding claims.
